hvtiRtables

Full reference documentation and worked examples: ehrlinger.github.io/hvtiRtables

You already know the drill: hand-copy a gtsummary table into a Word template, or run it through the SAS table macro, and by the third revision a footnote wording has drifted, a header has re-merged itself, or the font quietly changed. hvtiRtables closes that gap. Give it a gtsummary table object and you get back a .docx that already matches HVTI CORR’s “Table Construction for Manuscripts” rules (house font and rounding, footnotes and an abbreviation key as text below the table, no hidden spacer columns), the same way every time.

Tables are drawn in a style named by its role. A report table (hv_man_table()) is the working table of an analysis report. A manuscript table (hv_man_table(style = "manuscript")) is what a journal receives, laid out by what it does: "compare" for groups it compares, "describe" for cohorts or repeated measures it describes side by side.

The Table styles article draws one table in each and lists what differs.

Installation

hvtiRtables is part of the HVTI R family. Install it with the rest of the family through hvtiR:

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("ehrlinger/hvtiR")
hvtiR::install()

hvtiR::install() installs every member in one call, so the versions the members require of one another resolve together. Update later with hvtiR::update(), from a fresh R session: it will not overwrite a package that is already loaded.

To install hvtiRtables on its own:

pak::pak("ehrlinger/hvtiRtables")

Example 

library(gtsummary)
library(hvtiRtables)

tbl <- tbl_summary(trial, by = trt, include = c(age, grade))
ft <- hv_man_table(tbl)
hv_man_table_save(ft, "table1.docx")

For a manuscript submission, build the table with hv_tbl_summary(), which the manuscript style needs, name the style when shaping it, and give the saver the caption, which that style requires:

tbl <- hv_tbl_summary(
  trial, by = "trt",
  groups = list(Demography = "age", Disease = c("stage", "grade")),
  continuous = "age", categorical = c("stage", "grade")
)
ft <- hv_man_table(tbl, style = "manuscript")
hv_man_table_save(ft, "table1.docx", caption = "Table 1. Baseline Characteristics")

Describing cohorts side by side

A table that describes separate cohorts, or the same patients at several times, gives each group its own count. Name the layout:

ft <- hv_man_table(tbl, style = "manuscript", layout = "describe")
hv_man_table_save(ft, "table2.docx", caption = "Table 2. Cohorts")

hv_man_table_jtcvs(), hv_man_table_save_jtcvs() and hv_test_footnotes_jtcvs() are deprecated and go in the next release; their layout is this one.

Migrating from the %summarytable SAS macro

%summarytable computes the table and writes the document in one call. This package splits that into stages, so the parameters you know are spread across separate calls:

Stage Function Macro parameters
Compute hv_tbl_summary() CLASS=, CON*=, CAT*=, LIST=, PP=, PVALUES=, TOTALCOL=
Shape hv_man_table() STYLE= is style =; PAGE= has none (pages are US Letter)
Write hv_man_table_save*() RTFFILE=, ADDFN=, TBLTITLE= (caption)
Verify hv_check_docx() (no analogue)

The one thing worth knowing before you start: CON1= variables change statistic by default. The macro reported them as mean +/- SD with one-way ANOVA; every continuous variable here defaults to a median with a non-parametric test, which is the CON3= behavior. List a CON1= variable in normal as well as continuous to get the macro’s mean +/- SD and ANOVA back. It’s the largest of four defaults that produce different numbers from a faithful-looking port; the vignette’s “Defaults that differ” table lists all four.

For CORR tables, the standard dagger footnote follows continuous_stat and percentiles automatically through hv_man_table() and hv_man_table_save(). A mean table therefore says No. (%) or Mean±SD; a table showing both statistics names both. The (%) lives there and in the describe layout’s second header row, not in the cells, which print 12(39): no sign, as the SAS macro does, and no space, so a count and its percent are one word toward a journal’s limit.

Mean±SD cells follow Eugene H. Blackstone’s (EHB’s) paired rounding rule. The mean is rounded to the SD’s first-significant-digit place and the SD one place finer; an SD beginning with 1 gives both one additional place. Exact ties round to even, and so do those of medians and percentiles (62.5 shows as 62, where gtsummary and SAS showed 63). Medians and percentiles follow the house notation instead: brackets, 2 significant digits, and a value of 10 or more to the units place (102 [63, 170]). P values print without a leading zero (.013, <.001). A table that mixes mean and median marks the cells of the statistic fewer rows use (§ on medians, ¶ on means), with a note for each.

Full parameter map, the four defaults that differ, and the QNTLDEF quantile trap: Porting a %summarytable program to R.
